title.full: Global energy and climate outlook 2024 – Updating NDCs and closing the ambition gap – Indicators for 1.5°C alignment

description: Global normative pathway peaking at 1.5°C warming before declining to 1.3°C by 2100.
pathwayDescription:
The European Commission’s Global Energy and Climate Outlook 2024 (GECO) provides an ensemble of energy transition scenarios, developed by the Joint Research Centre. The 1.5°C scenario outlines a pathway to limit global temperature rise to 1.5°C by 2100, with a temporary overshoot to ~1.6 °C by mid-century. This is a significantly more ambitious outcome than the GECO Nationally Determined Contributions – Long Term Strategies (NDC-LTS) pathway, indicating that current national objectives fall significantly short of achieving this trajectory.

The 1.5°C pathway models a very rapid global transition, with accelerated decarbonization in electricity generation, strong electrification of end‐uses, efficiency improvements, decarbonization of hard-to-abate sectors (industry, long-haul transport, aviation etc.), and a scale up of negative emissions (land sink, carbon removal) to offset residual emissions. Emissions peak in the near term in this scenario, with sustained reductions reaching net-zero around 2060.

coreDrivers.policies: The scenario implements current and legislated policies as of July 2024, as in the accompanying Reference scenario. An additional high-ambition global uniform carbon price starts in 2025 and rises over time.
coreDrivers.emissionsTargets: Global pathway is constrained to limit warming to 1.5°C by 2100 with net zero around 2060 and negative emissions after that.
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: Technology learning rates are endogenously developed in the model, based on learning curve literature. The overall technology cost trend decreases based on the adoption of individual technologies and their unit costs.
coreDrivers.investmentChange: Annual power-sector investment doubles between 2020 and 2050, peaking in 2040. Solar and wind continue to dominate the technology mix, while storage becomes material from 2035 onward. Unabated fossil-fuel investment is no longer material by 2040, whereas CCS investment peaks in 2030 and remains material through 2050. Those investments increase GCP by 0.1% compared to reference scenario. As GDP also doubles over the same period, power-sector investment remains broadly constant as a share of GDP.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: Population and GDP assumptions are shared across the GECO scenarios and set the activity baseline. Inputs combine World Bank, IMF, OECD/SSP2, EU Ageing Report, and JRC-IIASA sources.
coreDrivers.behavioralShifts: The models assumed limited explicit behavioural-change modelling compared to Reference scenario. However, there is a general shift toward increased spending on low carbon heating and cooking appliances, as well as public transit.

dependencies.dependency_description: Building on existing legislated policies, this pathway adds a uniform global carbon price starting in 2025 to drive an 'economically efficient' reduction in emissions limiting warming to 1.5°C.
Least-cost optimization strongly shapes the power transition, with the global carbon price as a key driver influencing technology economics. However, the carbon price values are not published.
Significant renewable technology deployment implies additional grid flexibility and transmission infrastructure, but this is not quantified in the scenario.
Power-sector delivery depends on storage becoming cheaper and scaling sufficiently, and on CCS being deployable for residual fossil and biomass generation.

Renewable-power employment rises from 1.9 million jobs in 2020 to 11.9 million in 2035 and 17.2 million in 2050, implying substantial workforce scaling and reallocation. GECO does not identify specific shortages.
